extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, political economists, and students of public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Provide standards for assessing government bounties, premiums, drawbacks, and related trade regulations (especially export bounties and corn laws), focusing on their effects on prices, industry allocation, population, fiscal cost, domestic welfare, and international competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on population and domestic industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy (e.g., export bounty) that extends foreign consumption at the expense of the home market tends to restrain population and domestic industry and thereby reduces the long-run size of the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the measure shifts consumption abroad and thereby diminishes employment, population growth, and future domestic demand. Example: export bounties that increase foreign consumption of corn but reduce home consumption ultimately restrain industry and population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real versus nominal price effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounty commonly raises the nominal (money) price of a commodity without increasing its real value; it often acts by degrading the value of money (silver), so recipients gain mostly nominal, not real, benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether higher nominal receipts translate into greater real purchasing power (ability to buy labour and home-made goods). Example: a farmer selling at 4s vs 3s 6d may not be materially better off if 4s buys no more goods or labour than 3s 6d did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corn as the regulating commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: The money price of corn regulates the money price of labour and of most other home-produced commodities; therefore interventions affecting corn's money price ripple through wages, materials, and manufactured goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing policy, trace effects on wages, prices of raw produce and manufactures, and the overall cost structure of domestic industry. Smith uses corn as the benchmark commodity whose money price largely determines relative prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness in promoting actual production
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounty upon exportation does not necessarily increase the real production of the targeted commodity, because it may not enable producers to employ more labour or produce more real output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between incentives that raise nominal receipts and those that expand real productive capacity or labour employment. Prefer policies that demonstrably increase real output rather than only nominal price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficiary concentration and distributional impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Some interventions disproportionately benefit a narrow class (e.g., corn merchants, exporters) while imposing widespread tax burdens on the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which groups gain and which groups bear the cost; beware policies that chiefly enrich intermediaries (exporters/importers) while public bears the tax burden. Example: greatest zeal for bounties often comes from corn merchants who profit from increased trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market distortion via monopoly and price manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolies of the home market or export bounties can prevent markets from self-correcting (overstocking) and raise nominal prices without raising real value, producing distortions unlike those in ordinary manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the policy secures an artificial monopoly or prevents supply from smoothing price fluctuations between years, harming consumers and future production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitiveness and relative international prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that raise domestic nominal prices of commodities make domestic manufactures relatively dearer and foreign manufactures relatively cheaper, undermining domestic industries' competitiveness abroad and at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate international price effects and whether the policy enables foreign producers to undercut domestic producers in both foreign and home markets (e.g., Dutch example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misallocation of industry (forcing industry into worse channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile expedients (bounties, duties) tend to force parts of national industry into channels less advantageous than they would follow naturally, sometimes into entirely disadvantageous (losing) trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider opportunity costs and whether capital and labour are being diverted from more productive uses into subsidized but inefficient activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of bounty target: production versus exportation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties on production and on exportation have different effects: production bounties tend to lower home prices (and might refund some tax burden), whereas export bounties raise home nominal prices and are favoured by mercantile prejudice; production bounties may also be more fraud-prone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare which form aligns better with policy goals (lower consumer prices vs. encouraging exports) and weigh fraud/administrative risks. Note mercantile bias often explains preference for export bounties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance-based incentives versus capacity-based bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties proportional to capacity (e.g., tonnage bounties) reward ship size rather than actual performance or success, encouraging exploitation of the bounty rather than productive effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer rewards tied to measurable outcomes (catch, production, exports actually achieved) rather than simple metrics like tonnage that invite gaming and inefficiency. Example: herring busses claiming bounty with little catch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of policy to local geographic and technological conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A promoted mode of production or vessel type (borrowed from another country) may be ill-suited to local geography or practices, and bounties favoring it can destroy better-adapted local industries (e.g., buss-fishery vs. boat-fishery in Scotland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess local conditions (coastline, proximity, traditional techniques) and avoid one-size-fits-all incentives copied from other countries that reduce local welfare or employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on domestic affordability and the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that raise domestic prices of staple commodities harm the common people for whom such staples are important; bounties that divert produce abroad can raise home prices and reduce access for the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate distributional welfare impacts, particularly on staple affordability for low-income groups. Example: herring-bus bounty raised barrel prices, reducing supply to home market and hurting common people's food supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of speculative or incompetent entry
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous bounties often entice rash undertakers and joint-stock schemes who lack expertise, causing many to lose capital and producing little lasting industry improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether subsidies attract inexperienced entrants and lead to capital destruction; check historical outcomes (failed companies despite bounties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential evaluation: premiums versus bounties and drawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Public premiums to excellent artisans are less objectionable than broad bounties because they stimulate skill and quality without substantially distorting the allocation of capital; drawbacks (reimbursement of duties on exported goods in same form) are distinct and less problematic than bounties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor modest, targeted premiums that reward merit and craftsmanship; treat drawbacks as administrative reimbursement rather than a subsidy that changes production incentives. Semantic labels (premium, bounty, drawback) matter less than the economic substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: National defence and strategic-industry exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a manufacture is necessary for national defence and cannot otherwise be supported domestically, taxing other industries to support it may be defensible (e.g., sail-cloth, gunpowder bounties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow a narrow exception for strategic industries where self-sufficiency is essential for defence, but require strong justification and cost-benefit scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal cost and public burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties can impose very large costs on the public revenue and constitute heavy taxes on the population (example: the corn bounty sometimes costing over £300,000 in one year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always quantify the fiscal outlay and the distribution of that burden; compare public cost to actual public benefit and prefer policies with modest fiscal cost relative to clear public gains.
